program: Cradle-to-career services and Promise Academy charter schools in a 97-block Harlem zone

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/evidence-tier-batch-20261018/harlem-childrens-zone/acceptance.md — separately timed same-model source and model audit; not an independent second agent.

priceScope: HCZ spending per person served over six school years against adult earnings inferred from Promise Academy lottery math gains; income-only welfare comparison, not a verified marginal gift offer

what: Harlem Children’s Zone provides a pipeline of services, from parenting classes and early childhood through after-school, college support and family programs, across a 97-block area of Harlem.
It also runs the Promise Academy charter schools; HCZ reported serving 34,590 children and adults in FY22, 19,638 of them through its own programs.
This in-depth review prices HCZ’s spending per person served over six school years against the adult earnings implied by Promise Academy’s lottery-based math gains.
strengths: A lottery study of Promise Academy middle school applicants found math scores 0.283 standard deviations higher six years later; Arnold Ventures rates it Near Top Tier.
Admitted girls were about 10 points less likely to report a teen pregnancy (from 17%), and admitted boys’ incarceration fell from 4% to zero.
Lottery winners graduated high school on time 13 points more often and enrolled in college sooner.
reservations: Our working estimate is about $3.36M per better life; all of it is adult income inferred from test scores, and we do not credit the teen-pregnancy or incarceration effects.
The lottery sample was small (407 students), and J-PAL reports no difference in six-year graduation or in ever enrolling in college.
The central case treats the charter school’s public funding as replacing district spending; counting it would raise the estimate several-fold.

sections.what: Harlem Children’s Zone (Harlem Childrens Zone Inc, EIN 23-7112974) aims to support children from birth through college in a 97-block area of central Harlem, with parenting workshops, early-childhood programs, after-school and summer programs, health and family services, and college and career support. Its Promise Academy charter schools are separate legal entities funded mainly by public per-pupil payments. HCZ reported 34,590 people served in FY22, including 19,638 through its own programming. A donation to HCZ supports its non-charter programs.
sections.monitoring: Dobbie and Fryer used Promise Academy’s 2005 and 2006 sixth-grade admission lotteries (150 winners, 257 non-winners) and surveyed participants in 2012, near the end of high school. HCZ publishes annual impact reports with counts served. We did not find current Promise Academy enrollment or a cost per student; we have not contacted the organization.
sections.qualitative: Lottery winners scored 0.283 standard deviations higher on a nationally normed math test six years after admission. They were 13 points more likely to graduate high school in four years (58% baseline), though not within six years, and enrolled in college sooner but not more often overall, according to J-PAL’s summary. Female winners reported about 10 points fewer teen pregnancies (17% baseline), and male winners’ incarceration was zero against 4%. There were no differences in drug or alcohol use or in self-reported health. The working paper abstract reports a larger college effect (14.1 points); we follow the more conservative published summary.
sections.cost:
Our central estimate is **$3.36M per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. It is an income-only comparison: we credit no health gain and do not value the teen-pregnancy or incarceration effects.

**Cost.** HCZ’s FY2023 expense was $117.3M, about $5,975 per person served by its own programs. We charge that for six school years per Promise Academy student, $35,850, and treat the charter school’s public per-pupil funding as replacing what the district would otherwise spend.

**Benefit.** The 0.283 SD math gain is about 11 percentile points; at Chetty et al.’s $150 a year per percentile, that implies about $2,340 a year in 2025 dollars. We treat half as causal, 60% as net welfare, from age 25 to 59 on a $35,000 base, with 0.9 for displacement and 0.8 for NYC residence.

**Range.** Adding the charter school’s own spending gives $14.59M per better life; charging all HCZ spending to charter students gives $43.99M per better life. If the full association is causal, $1.68M per better life. If the test gains never reach adult earnings, there is no credited benefit.
sections.funding: Harlem Childrens Zone Inc reported FY2023 (June) expenses of $117.3M, up from $104.3M in FY2022, after $152.5M in FY2021, funded almost entirely by contributions ($98.3M in FY2023). The Promise Academy charter entity reported $29.9M of expenses in FY2023. We have not seen a costed plan for adding students or services.

model.costScope: HCZ Inc FY2023 expense per person served (own programs) × six school years; charter per-pupil funding excluded as displacing district spending.
model.geographicAttribution: Harlem students; 0.8 of adult earning years in the NYC metro.
model.formula: Price = 10 × (HCZ cost per person × 6) ÷ [0.5 × discounted years(ages 25–59 from 12) × ln(1 + 0.6 × gain ÷ base) × causal × non-displacement × NYC share]. Gain = 0.283 SD × 37.5 percentiles/SD × $150 × CPI. Health = 0.
model.counterfactual: Lottery losers in other NYC schools.
model.attribution: A gift is credited with the average Promise Academy effect per student at HCZ’s average per-person cost; other HCZ programs unquantified.
model.uncertainty: Dominated by the test-score-to-earnings link and by whether charter public funding is a real added cost.
model.nativeOutcomes: Math scores, on-time graduation, college enrollment timing, teen pregnancy, incarceration and health self-reports.
